verdicts.trueWording: Except Brian Vastag was very much alive
verdicts.note: Live raw fetch of theverge.com (HTTP 200). Quote is word for word in the opening paragraphs; the same passage says the fake obituaries had leapt to the top of Google Search results, that Mazur alone had died, and a later paragraph says the sites have hallmarks of AI generation. All limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: repeating inaccurate details, like where Mazur lived
verdicts.note: Raw page. Sentence reads that the obituaries are detached and nearly identical, with a few words moved around, then the quoted clause. AI-generation limb carried by the preceding sentence about hallmarks of AI tools. 'each repeated the same' is a fair reading of the collective plural, not a separate assertion on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: they lack quotes from family or friends of the deceased
verdicts.note: Raw page, The Thaiger section. Preceding sentence says content on that site has hallmarks of being generated using artificial intelligence, so the 'generated' limb holds.
Raw page, The Thaiger section. Same sentence states the articles are written like typical obituaries and news articles, supporting the news-article-form limb.

verdicts.trueWording: the curious and concerned public is advised to stay tuned
verdicts.note: Raw page, The Thaiger section: Sato quotes one sentence from an article on the death of a Calgary, Canada woman, telling readers updates are anticipated and to stay tuned for verified information. The page never says the sentence closes the article, so the 'ends by' limb is unsupported; every other limb (Calgary woman, AI-hallmarked site, awaiting verified information) is on the page.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that the quoted sentence ends the article

verdicts.trueWording: appears to be an AI summary of the op-ed
verdicts.note: Raw page. Sato's parenthetical follows Vastag's suspicion that someone scraped an op-ed he and Mazur co-authored; the opening establishes Mazur as the one who actually died.

Live raw fetch of wired.com (HTTP 200), opening section. Echovita published a summary of the obituary the husband and stepdaughter wrote; the automation limb rests on the article's own account of a web-crawling company plus the widower's line about their algorithm or program.

verdicts.trueWording: her children weren't mentioned as survivors
verdicts.note: Raw page, opening section, the sentence directly after the granddaughter/grandson line; same Echovita summary.

verdicts.trueWording: failing to note that they were dogs
verdicts.note: Raw page, opening section. The summary called Tug and Cash her close friends; the family obituary had described her two dogs by name.

verdicts.trueWording: an incoherent and oddly hostile obituary for former NBA player
verdicts.note: Live raw fetch of wired.com (HTTP 200), closing section. Knibbs writes that Microsoft's MSN news site was roundly castigated for it, naming Brandon Hunter.

verdicts.trueWording: critics assumed the garbled article was written by AI
verdicts.note: Raw page, same closing section; the parenthetical that follows says Microsoft never confirmed whether the story was AI-generated, though it was removed. Both limbs supported.

Live raw fetch of legalgenealogist.com (HTTP 200), MyHeritage section. Russell quotes the amended Limited Use License and says these limits had not been there before. Note the licence text grants use of 'the Service and the Website'; the claim's 'its records' is a gloss, though the same post lists historical records among the covered data.

verdicts.trueWording: easily generate lovely bios with lots of false
verdicts.note: Live raw fetch of wikitree.com (HTTP 200 with browser headers; the plain fetch returned an empty 202). Question body attributes the wording to Brad Foley from Canada Project discussions; the page's next word is the scare-quoted 'facts'.

verdicts.trueWording: A single footnote meets current standards, but is clearly not enough
verdicts.note: Same question body, one sentence later than index 959. The preceding sentence supplies the thirty lines and forty-five statements; the clause continues that it cannot support such a long biography, which might be loaded with hallucinated facts.

verdicts.trueWording: was a loving mother, she always looked after her children
verdicts.note: Raw page, the +18-vote answer by M Ross, Nov 23 2023. M Ross introduces it as an example with a made up name of the kind of prose AI generates, so 'parody line' is a characterisation of an illustrative example rather than the page's own word.
